BEFORE THE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
                           OF THE STATE OF MISSOURI

 In the Matter of the Application of Evergy    )
 Metro, Inc. d/b/a Evergy Missouri Metro’s     )
                                                 File No. ER-2026-0143
 Request for Authority to Implement a          )
 General Rate Increase for Electric Service.   )

                                         REPLY BRIEF

          Pursuant to the March 18, 2026 Order Setting Procedural Schedule and Directing the

Filing Dates for Local Public Hearings (“Order Setting Procedural Schedule”), Google LLC

(“Google”), hereby files its Reply Brief. The Commission should approve the LLPS Partial

Stipulation and Agreement (“LLPS Stipulation”) in its entirety without any modifications or

changes and that the LLPS Stipulation is just and reasonable in the public interest, (2) reject

modifications to the Large Load Power Service (“LLPS”) Tariff proposed by the Office of the

Public Counsel (“OPC”) and (3) preserve the integrated framework for the Fuel Adjustment Clause

(“FAC”), thereby rejecting Staff’s proposals to impose separate, wholesale-market-based

treatment of LLPS customers. Google further requests that the Commission reject OPC’s proposal

to assign all costs associated with Mullin Creek #2 exclusively to LLPS customers, as well as

OPC’s proposed Probability of Dispatch (“POD”) methodology for allocating generation and

transmission costs, both of which are inconsistent with cost-causation principles and unsupported

by the evidentiary record.

 I. Introduction

         1.    Google’s Reply Brief addresses the principal arguments and the most significant

concerns raised in the Initial Post-Hearing Briefs filed by the Office of the Public Counsel

(“OPC”), Staff of the Public Service Commission of the State of Missouri (“Staff”), Midwest

Energy Consumers Group (“MECG”), and Velvet Tech Services, LLC (“Velvet”). To the extent

any issue is not specifically addressed herein, such omission should not be construed as agreement

with or acquiescence to OPC, Staff’s, MECG’s or Velvet’s position.

II. The LLPS Stipulation’s Treatment of the FAC Results in Just and Reasonable Rates.

         A.    There Is No Mismatch in the Calculation of the Base Factor

         2.    Staff’s Initial Brief argues that the LLPS Stipulation creates a mismatch between

the base factor calculation and the operation of the fuel adjustment clause (“FAC”) going forward.1

Specifically, Staff claims that it is problematic to exclude LLPS expense and billing determinants

(load) from the calculation of the FAC base factor, but then includes LLPS expenses and billing

determinants in the calculation of the FAC fuel adjustment rate (“FAR”) going forward.2

         3.    However, what Staff characterizes as a mismatch is really just a function of the

timing of this proceeding relative to the initiation of service to LLPS customers. As Staff notes,

Commission Rule 20 CSR 4240-20.090(2) requires rebasing of base energy costs in a general rate

proceeding in which an FAC is continued or modiﬁed.3 There were no LLPS customers in the test

year and no LLPS energy costs are being rebased in the Company’s revenue requirement.4

Consistent with Staff’s position that the FAC base factor must match the base energy costs in the

energy costs and billing determinants.6 Accordingly, the FAC base factor in the LLPS Stipulation

matches the base energy costs in the revenue requirement.

         4.    The FAC base factor is the starting point for the FAC FAR going forward. As is

the case whenever the FAC base factor is set, customers come and go (or consume more or less)

and energy costs evolve during the accumulation period, but as long as the energy costs in the FAC

base factor match the base energy costs in the revenue requirement, the FAC base factor is properly

set to recover actual energy costs.

         5.    While it is true that the LLPS Stipulation permits actual LLPS energy costs to enter

the FAC during future accumulation periods, LLPS billing determinants will also enter the FAC.

Accordingly, LLPS customers will pay their share of the FAC FAR, just like all other customers.7

Staff claims, without supporting evidence, that non-LLPS customers will be exposed to the cost

of serving new LLPS load through the FAC. Staff does not explain why it believes increased

energy costs flowing through the FAC will not be entirely absorbed by the increased billing

determinants (i.e., kilowatt-hours) supplied by LLPS customers, over which the energy costs will

be allocated. In fact, with the premium rates paid by LLPS customers and the contributions of

LLPS customers to a more efficient system, energy costs per kilowatt-hour may very well decrease

due to the participation of LLPS customers in the FAC.8

          B.    The 90/10 Sharing Mechanism Increases Benefits to Non-LLPS Customers

         6.    Currently, the FAC includes a 95/5 sharing mechanism by which incremental FAC

costs are paid 95% by the customers and 5% by Evergy. The LLPS Stipulation increases the

portion of incremental FAC costs to be paid by Evergy. Specifically, incremental FAC costs will

be allocated between non-LLPS and LLPS customers based upon kWh usage for the period over

which the incremental FAC costs, if any, were incurred. After this allocation, incremental allocated

non-LLPS FAC costs shall be shared utilizing the existing 95/5 sharing mechanism and

incremental allocated LLPS FAC costs shall be shared utilizing 90/10 sharing mechanism.9 After

the Evergy share is subtracted, the allocated amounts will be totaled and used to develop the current

period FAR.10 Thus, all customers, including non-LLPS customers will benefit from the new

90/10 sharing mechanism.11

         7.    The 90/10 sharing arrangement in the LLPS Stipulation increases the likelihood

that LLPS customers’ participation in the FAC will decrease energy costs paid by non-LLPS

customers. Staff attempts to minimize the impact of the 90/10 sharing mechanism with a selective

calculation in Attachment A to its Objection to the LLPS Stipulation (On-the-Record Presentation

Ex. 2).12 But Staff’s calculation assumes a small fuel adjustment rate and a hypothetical scenario

in which LLPS customers are 10% of the total load.13 As LLPS customers ramp up and if they

exceed 10% of the total load, the 90/10 sharing mechanism will become more impactful.

          C.    Staff’s Option 1 Creates a Mismatch Between the Revenue Requirement and
               Base Factor and Makes Flawed Assumptions regarding LMPs

         8.    As explained above, the calculation of the FAC base factor in the LLPS Stipulation

is consistent with the exclusion of LLPS costs from the revenue requirement. Conversely, Staff

supports excluding LLPS costs from the revenue requirement but including LLPS energy costs and

kilowatt-hours in its calculation of the FAC base factor in its Option 1.14 This mismatch violates

Staff’s rule about the FAC base factor matching the revenue requirement.

         9.    To make matters worse, Staff uses an improper methodology to include LLPS

energy costs and kilowatt-hours in its calculation of the FAC base factor in its Option 1. As

discussed in Google’s Initial Brief, to reach an estimated annualized energy expense for Option 1,

Staff relied on normalized and annualized day-ahead locational marginal prices (“LMPs”)

produced by the SPP Integrated Marketplace.15 Staff also made inadequately supported

assumptions about LLPS customer usage and load factors as part of its normalized and annualized

day-ahead LMP calculations.16

III. The LLPS Revenue Adjustment of $60 Million is Grounded in Actual, Corrected Billing
    Information and Provides an Immediate Benefit to Customers.

         13.   The $60 million revenue adjustment in the LLPS Stipulation is grounded in actual

billing information, corrected to reflect the proper application of the Commission-approved LLPS

Tariff, rather than speculative estimates of future customer demand. The adjustment was derived

from the actual billing determinants for the LLPS customer as of the June 30, 2026 true-up date,

annualized to reflect twelve months of service at that level.27 This approach is consistent with

traditional ratemaking principles, which annualize known and measurable changes occurring

during the true-up period. Unlike Staff’s and OPC’s alternatives, the $60 million adjustment does

not depend upon assumptions about when an LLPS customer will achieve future contracted

capacity or projected levels of electricity consumption.

         14.   The $60 million adjustment also incorporates a correction to the calculation of

minimum monthly bills under the LLPS Tariff—a correction that Google advocated for even

though it increases Google’s own payment obligations. As Dr. Berry explained, the tariff

establishes a monthly Billing Demand equal to the greater of the customer’s measured maximum

demand or 80% of annual Contract Capacity.28 The resulting Demand Charge is payable in

addition to the tariff's other applicable charges, including energy-based charges.29 Evergy’s earlier

         15.   Velvet characterizes the correction to the minimum bill calculation as a

         17.   The $60 million adjustment strikes the appropriate balance by recognizing

substantial, demonstrable benefits from LLPS customers today without embedding speculative or

unbalanced assumptions into the revenue requirement. The adjustment immediately reduces the

amount that must otherwise be recovered from existing customers, even though no LLPS customer

was included in the test year and no new generation or transmission investment attributable to the

LLPS customer is reflected in the revenue requirement in this case.


IV. The Stipulated Earnings Review and Sharing Mechanism is a Reasonable Protection
    Against Future Excess Earnings.

         18.   The ERS Mechanism established by the LLPS Stipulation represents a reasonable,

balanced approach to protecting existing customers while preserving Evergy’s incentive to attract

and serve new large loads. As Google explained in its Initial Brief, this is a transitional rate case

in which no LLPS customers were included in the historical test year, and significant additional

LLPS revenue growth is expected after rates become effective.36 The ERS Mechanism addresses

that circumstance through two objective conditions: (1) Evergy’s actual earned return on equity

rate revenues must exceed the LLPS revenues reflected in the revenue requirement established in

this case. If both conditions are satisfied, 65% of the qualifying excess earnings, after the

applicable tax gross-up, will be deferred as a regulatory liability for the benefit of retail customers,

with 15 percentage points of the total excess earnings designated for low-income customers.37

         19.     The ERS Mechanism established by the LLPS Stipulation supplements the $60

million LLPS revenue adjustment already reducing the revenue requirement in this case. It

therefore provides existing customers both an immediate benefit from known LLPS revenues and

an opportunity to share in additional earnings associated with future LLPS growth, without relying

on speculative assumptions about future load development.

         20.     Staff advocates for essentially the same framework as the ERS Mechanism

reflected in the LLPS Stipulation: two-trigger approach involving LLPS revenue growth and

companywide earned ROE, and a 65% customer-sharing percentage.38 However, Staff takes issue

with the 20-basis-point retention allowance proposed in the LLPS Stipulation.39 The modest

deadband appropriately recognizes that an authorized ROE represents an opportunity to earn a

reasonable return, not a guaranteed level of earnings, while preserving an incentive for Evergy to

pursue load growth that will ultimately benefit all customers. As Evergy explained, the deadband

also avoids undue differences in incentives between its Missouri and Kansas jurisdictions.40

         21.     OPC’s primary position is that the Commission should adopt its $117 million LLPS

revenue adjustment, in which case an earnings sharing mechanism would not be required.41

         22.    MECG’s proposed two-way LLPS revenue tracker is similarly flawed because it

V. OPC has not Demonstrated that all Mullin Creek #2 Costs Should be Assigned
   Exclusively to LLPS Customers.

         24.   Mullin Creek #2 is a 440-MW simple-cycle natural-gas turbine generating facility

under construction in Nodaway County, about 94 miles northwest of Kansas City. It is currently

under review in a pending Certificate of Convenience and Necessity (“CCN”) proceeding.46 As

Evergy explains in that proceeding, “[t]he [p]roject is a key part of Evergy’s plans to achieve the

preferred solution to meet the energy and reliability needs of the Company’s customers over the

twenty-year planning horizon of its Integrated Resource Plan.”47

         25.   Before reaching the question of how to allocate the construction work in progress

(“CWIP”) expense associated with Mullin Creek #2, the Commission must first determine if such

CWIP is recoverable in this case. Google does not take a position on this threshold issue. However,

if the Commission permits recovery of CWIP associated with Mullin Creek #2 in this case, it

should be allocated using the established A&E 4-CP Methodology. The Commission should reject

OPC’s recommendation that all CWIP associated with Mullin Creek #2 be allocated to LLPS

customers.48

         26.   OPC’s recommendation is contrary to the evidence that Mullin Creek #2 is a

system-wide asset.49 OPC does not provide any evidence that the need for Mullin Creek #2 is

VI. OPC’s Proposed Probability of Dispatch Methodology Fails to Account for Capacity
    Related Cost Causation and Risks Distorting Future LLPS Cost Allocations.

         30.   OPC’s proposed Probability of Dispatch (“POD”) methodology also raises

significant concerns regarding the allocation of generation and transmission costs among customer

classes. As reflected in OPC’s Initial Brief, its POD methodology would increase the allocation to

the Large Power Service (“LPS”) class from 12.9% to 19.3% and to the Large General Service

(“LGS”) class from 18.6% to 23.9%, while reducing the residential allocation from 46.3% to

34.5%.54 Although the allocation methodology would not immediately impact LLPS customers

because there is no LLPS load in the test year, these substantial rate shifts would materialize in

future cost-of-service studies.

         31.    More fundamentally, OPC’s methodology fails to adequately reflect the costs that

actually drive generation and transmission investment. As Google witness Dr. Berry explained,

generation and transmission facilities are constructed to meet peak demand and capacity

requirements, not simply to supply energy during the hours in which generating resources are

dispatched.55 Although energy-related factors contribute to certain costs, Evergy’s existing A&E

4-CP methodology already accounts for both energy and capacity-related cost drivers.56

          32.    By contrast, OPC’s POD methodology relies exclusively on hourly energy usage

and fails to capture what Dr. Berry identified as the most significant driver of generation costs:

capacity needs.57 Evaluating all 8,760 hours of the year does not cure this deficiency because it

dilutes the critical peak-demand signals that drive capacity investment and resource-adequacy

planning.58 Dr. Berry further testified that OPC provided no meaningful support for applying POD

to transmission costs.59 Accordingly, the Commission should reject OPC’s proposed POD

methodology and retain the established A&E 4-CP methodology, which more appropriately

reflects the capacity and energy requirements underlying generation and transmission cost

causation.


VII.     Conclusion & Requested Relief

         33.    WHEREFORE, Google LLC respectfully requests the Commission approve the

LLPS Stipulation in its entirety. Approval of the LLPS Stipulation will promote regulatory

certainty, advance the public interest, and facilitate continued investment in the state. Google

remains committed to working collaboratively with all stakeholders and the Commission to

address the integration of large loads into Evergy’s system and to ensure Missouri is well-

positioned among states competing for data center and AI investment, while benefiting existing

electric consumers and the public interest.
